summary: Defines the Mobile IPv6 MIB, used to monitor and control the mobile node, home agent, and correspondent node functions of a Mobile IPv6 entity. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A dashboard for checking on moving devices and their home bases.

subtitle: The SNMP data model for watching and controlling Mobile IPv6 mobile nodes, home agents and correspondent nodes.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to monitor and configure the Mobile IPv6 functions of mobile nodes, home agents and correspondent nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The MOBILEIPV6-MIB defines SNMP managed objects in groups for common data (mip6Core), mobile nodes (mip6Mn), correspondent nodes (mip6Cn) and home agents (mip6Ha), plus notifications.
tldr.outcome: Management stations can read bindings, counters and lists, and set a few parameters, using one standard module registered as mib-2 number 133. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4295 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Managing Mobile IPv6 Entities
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) lets nodes stay reachable while moving around the IPv6 Internet. RFC 4295 defines a set of managed objects in a Management Information Base (MIB) to monitor and control any entity that implements it. It is written for the Internet-Standard Management Framework, where MIB objects are generally accessed through SNMP and defined with SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580).

Three kinds of entity are covered. A mobile node (MN) can change its point of attachment from one link to another while staying reachable via its home address. A correspondent node (CN) is a peer the mobile node is talking to, and it does not necessarily need Mobile IPv6 support. A home agent (HA) is a router on the mobile node's home link that holds the mobile node's registered care-of address and forwards intercepted packets to it.
sections.eli5: Think of a pen pal who keeps moving house. The post office at their old home (the home agent) forwards the mail. This memo is the checklist a manager uses to see how all of that is going.

sections.title: What Must Be Monitored and Controlled
sections.content:
The RFC lists what a manager needs to see: the capabilities of Mobile IPv6 entities, traffic due to Mobile IPv6, binding-related statistics and binding details, and the history of Binding Updates. The statistics and history apply at the home agent, correspondent node and mobile node as appropriate.

It also lists parameters that the Mobile IPv6 specification says should be manually configurable. Examples are the preference value and lifetime a home agent uses in Router Advertisements, whether it sends ICMP Mobile Prefix Advertisements, whether it answers ICMP Mobile Prefix Solicitation messages, and whether it processes multicast group membership control messages from mobile nodes.
sections.eli5: A manager wants to know who is where, how much mail is moving, and to change a few settings, like how loudly a home base announces itself.

sections.title: MIB Design and Groups
sections.content:
The design principle is to keep the MIB as simple as possible while meeting the essential monitoring and control needs. Where possible, existing MIBs (such as the IPSec MIB, Neighbor Discovery MIB and Tunnel MIB, RFC 4087) are meant to be used instead. The MOBILEIPV6-MIB is assumed to always be implemented together with the IPv6-capable IP-MIB (RFC 4293), and it uses textual conventions from RFC 4001.

The module is split into groups: mip6Core for objects common to all entities, mip6Ha for the home agent service, mip6Mn for the mobile node (including Dynamic Home Agent discovery and records of movement), mip6Cn for the correspondent node (mainly its part in the Return Routability procedure), and mip6Notifications for asynchronous alerts.
sections.eli5: The dashboard has one panel for things everybody shares, and separate panels for the moving device, its friend, and the home base.

sections.title: Tables and Key Objects
sections.content:
The mip6BindingCacheTable models the binding cache kept by home agents and correspondent nodes. Each row is one accepted Binding Update, indexed by home address type and home address, and holds the care-of address, time registered, time granted and remaining (in seconds), and whether it is a home registration. The mip6BindingAdminStatus object is read-write: an operator can change an entry from active to inactive, which deletes it, but changing it back is rejected. The mip6BindingHistoryTable tracks the history of the cache.

Other tables include mip6NodeTrafficTable (per mobile node traffic counters), mip6MnHomeAddressTable (home addresses and registration state), mip6MnBLTable (the mobile node's Binding Update List), mip6CnCounterTable and mip6HaCounterTable (registration statistics), mip6HaConfTable (advertisement parameters per interface), mip6HaListTable (routers acting as home agents on each link) and mip6HaGlAddrTable (home agent global addresses).

The mobile node state object mip6MnHomeAddressState takes the values unknown, home, registered, pending and isolated. A textual convention, Mip6BURequestRejectionCode, maps 12 rejection reasons to the Binding Acknowledgment status codes 128 to 139 of RFC 3775.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a set of spreadsheets: one lists who is registered where, one keeps old entries, and others count messages. A few cells can be edited by the manager.

sections.title: Notifications and Conformance
sections.content:
Five notifications let managed entities report events asynchronously: mip6MnRegistered, mip6MnDeRegistered, mip6MnCOAChanged, mip6MnBindingExpiredAtHA and mip6MnBindingExpiredAtCN.

The module ends with groups and many compliance statements, so an implementation can claim support for just one role, such as home agent or correspondent node, and for read-only operation where write access is not required. The compliance text notes that the home address objects must support global IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: Notifications are like a doorbell that rings when a device arrives, leaves or moves. Compliance statements say which parts of the dashboard a product must include.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several read-write objects are sensitive: mip6Status (enables or disables Mobile IPv6), mip6HaAdvPreference and mip6HaAdvLifetime (could push mobile nodes to choose the wrong home agent or use wrong lifetimes), mip6BindingAdminStatus, mip6HaPrefixAdv, mip6HaPrefixSolicitation and mip6HaMCastCtlMsgSupport. Setting them without protection can disrupt Mobile IPv6 communication.

Readable objects can also leak information. Care-of address objects reveal the location and movement of a mobile node, and the correspondent address objects reveal who a mobile node is talking to. Because SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, the RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The dashboard shows where people are and has switches that can break things. So only trusted people with a secret key should be allowed to look or touch.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned a base arc in the mib-2 tree for the mip6MIB module identity. The mib-2 number is 133.

The module's initial version is dated 1 February 2006, and the RFC was published in April 2006.
sections.eli5: Every dashboard needs a unique address in the big phone book of network objects. This one got number 133.

viz.caption: MAIN GROUPS OF THE MOBILE IPV6 MIB (RFC 4295)

items.label: unknown
items.desc: State of the mobile node cannot be determined.

items.label: home
items.desc: Mobile node is on the home network.

items.label: registered
items.desc: On a foreign network and registered with the home agent.

items.label: pending
items.desc: Registration request sent, waiting for the reply.

items.label: isolated
items.desc: Not at home, not registered, no registration ack pending.
